summary: Gérard Colas specializes in Indology and religious studies. He has served as Directeur de recherche at the CNRS, attested in 2004 and 2009, as well as at the Centre d'Études de l'Inde et de l'Asie du Sud in 2012.

Gérard Fussman studied at the École Normale Supérieure from around 1961 to 1965, working in Indology, history and archaeology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. In 1984, he became a professor at the Collège de France, succeeding Jean Filliozat.
Active in computational fields, Indology, and linguistics, Gérard Huet studied under George Ernst (ca. 1970–1972) and Maurice Nivat (ca. 1972–1976). He was appointed a professor at Inria around 1972.

Géza Bethlenfalvy studied at Eötvös Loránd University and under Lajos Ligeti. Working in Tibetology, Indology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies, he held posts at the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, University of Delhi, Eötvös Loránd University, and University of Vienna.

Gösta Liebert studied at Lund and Gothenburg under Hjalmar Frisk, Nils Holmer, and Stig Wikander. An Indology and linguistics scholar, he held posts at Lund University, Uppsala University (1951–1953), and as professor at Gothenburg University (1955–1982).

Götz von Selle studied at Berlin, Kiel, and Göttingen. A historian and Central Asian specialist, he worked at the Göttingen and Berlin state libraries before becoming a professor at the University of Göttingen (1938) and the University of Königsberg (ca. 1938–1945).

Günter Grönbold is a scholar of Indology, Tibetology, and Buddhist studies. He had a long career at the Bavarian State Library from around 1974 to 2008, where he served as head of the Oriental Section from around 1988 to 2008.

Günter Schweiger studied at Vienna University of Economics and Business and under Gert Klingenschmitt. A scholar of linguistics and Iranian/Central Asian studies, he was an assistant at Linz and served as a full university professor at WU Vienna (1974–2009).

H. Craig Melchert studied at Michigan State University, the Defense Language Institute, the National Cryptologic School, and Harvard University. A linguist, he held academic positions at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (1978–2007) and UCLA (2007–2015).

Indologist H. G. Narahari studied at the University of Mysore and the University of Madras, completing an MA under C. Kunhan Raja. In 1944, he was attested as a Research Fellow at Madras and a Research Assistant at the Adyar Library.

H. V. Nagaraja Rao is a scholar of Indology, linguistics, and philosophy. He has held positions at the Oriental Research Institute Mysore and served as a professor at the University of Mysore (attested 2012).
Haeju Sunim is a Buddhist studies scholar. She served as a visiting lecturer at Harvard University from 1996 to 1997 and was an Associate Professor of Buddhist Studies at Dongguk University in 1999.

Haiyan Hu-von Hinüber studied at Peking University under Zhongxin Jiang and Kemu Jin, specializing in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Sinology. In 2010, she served as the Director of the Confucius Institute at the University of Freiburg.

Kitamura studied at the University of Tokyo under Tokan Tada. Working in linguistics and Tibetology, he held posts at the National Institute for Japanese Language, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies, Reitaku University as president, and served as Toyo Bunko's board chairman.

Hajime Nakamura studied at the University of Tokyo, specializing in Indology, Buddhist studies, and philosophy. He became a professor at the University of Tokyo (1954–1973), founded Toho Gakuin and the Eastern Institute, and served as director of both institutions.

Hajime Okayama studied at Kyoto University, University of Tokyo, CASS, and Peking University under Xianlin Ji. A specialist in Buddhist studies, philosophy, and Sinology, he was a professor at the University of Tokyo from 1995 to 2012.

Hajime Sakurabe studied at Otani University under Issai Funahashi and Susumu Yamaguchi, focusing on Buddhist studies and Indology. He held various academic positions at Otani University, including professor from 1971 to 1986, and taught at Nava Nalanda Mahavihara.

Hajime Tanabe studied at Tokyo, Kyoto, Berlin, and Freiburg under Raphael von Koeber, Kitaro Nishida, Martin Heidegger, and Heinrich Rickert. A philosopher, he taught at Tohoku University and served as an assistant professor at Kyoto University from 1919 to 1945.
Hakuin Ekaku was a scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy who studied under Dōkyō Etan around 1708 and Hakuyūshi around 1710–1711, later teaching Suiō Genro.

Hakuju Ui studied at Tokyo under Junjiro Takakusu, and at Oxford, Cambridge, and Tübingen under Richard von Garbe. An Indology and Buddhist studies scholar, he taught at Tokyo and Tohoku universities and became president of Komazawa University in 1941.
